title: How to Choose an AI Condition Monitoring Provider
summary: Seven criteria for choosing an AI condition monitoring provider: sensor coverage, retrofit options, SLAs, edge deployment, and CMMS and ERP integration.
body_markdown:
## Key Points


- Two providers can run similar AI models and still deliver very different results, because installation, connectivity, integration, support, and contract terms decide whether alerts turn into repairs.
- Evaluate providers on seven criteria: multimodal sensor coverage, edge deployment, retrofit capability, CMMS and ERP integration, SLA terms, support model, and pricing transparency.
- Use the scorecard and pilot steps at the end to compare two or three finalists on your own assets before signing a multi-year contract.


An AI condition monitoring provider supplies the[industrial IoT sensors](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/industrial-iot-sensors) , connectivity, software, and people that turn machine signals into maintenance decisions. Feature lists across providers look similar; what separates them is how they install on your oldest pumps, how their alerts reach your planners, and who picks up the phone when a technician doubts a call.


The seven criteria below are written as questions you can put to each provider, with what a strong answer looks like.


## Criterion 1: Multimodal Sensor Coverage


Choose a provider whose sensors measure the signals your critical failure modes actually produce, because that decides which[equipment failure](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/equipment-failure) patterns the AI can see at all. Vibration alone catches many mechanical faults, but early lubrication problems, electrical faults, and slow-speed bearing wear often show up first in ultrasound, current, or temperature.


Multimodal monitoring combines those signals so one alert can separate causes that look alike on a single channel. Take a centrifugal pump with rising vibration: the cause could be a bearing defect, cavitation from low suction pressure, or misalignment after a motor swap. Ultrasound, current, and spectral data together narrow it down before anyone opens the pump.


Ask each provider:


- Which signals does one sensor measure natively, and at what frequency range?
- Which signals need a second device or a partner product?
- Can it monitor electrical health (current, voltage, power) on the same asset?


A strong answer maps signals to your top failure modes, not to a generic spec sheet. For background on the method most platforms start from, see[industrial vibration analysis](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/industrial-vibration-analysis) .


## Criterion 2: Edge Deployment and Connectivity


Pick a provider whose data path fits your network rules, because connectivity is where many projects stall in IT review. Ask where processing happens (on the sensor, a gateway, or the cloud) and how data leaves the plant floor.


Systems whose gateways send data over cellular avoid touching the plant network, which can shorten security review considerably. Systems that route data through the plant LAN may need firewall rules, switch ports, or OT network approvals at each site.


**Ask each provider:**


- Does the system need plant Wi-Fi, Ethernet, or OT network access?
- What happens to readings during a connectivity outage?
- Which detection steps run locally, and which run in the cloud?
- What security certifications does the provider hold (for example, SOC 2 or ISO 27001)?


Our guide to[edge AI for industrial plants](https://tractian.com/en/blog/edge-ai-industrial-plants) covers edge, cloud, and hybrid architectures in more depth.


## Criterion 3: Retrofit Capability for Legacy Equipment


Choose a provider that can instrument the machines you have today, including assets with no nameplate data, tight access, washdown exposure, or hazardous area classification. Most condition monitoring programs are retrofits, so this criterion often decides how much of your fleet you can actually cover.


Ask each provider:


- What mounting options exist (stud, epoxy pad, magnet), and which do they recommend for high-frequency bearing detection?
- Can sensors be installed while the machine runs?
- What environment ratings do the sensors carry (temperature range, IP rating, Class 1 Div 1)?
- How does the provider set up fault frequencies when bearing part numbers are unknown?


A strong provider asks for your asset list and criticality ranking before quoting, then proposes sensing points per machine. Tractian, for example, maps how each critical asset fails and which signals catch it earliest, then validates conditions on-site before finalizing scope.


## Criterion 4: CMMS and ERP Integration


Select a provider whose alerts land in the system your planners already use, with enough detail to plan the job. An alert stuck in a separate dashboard tends to be read late or not at all.


**Ask each provider:**


- Are there prebuilt connectors for your CMMS or ERP (for example, SAP, IBM Maximo, or Oracle NetSuite)?
- Is there an open API, and who maintains the integration after your system upgrades?
- Does the work order carry the asset ID, fault, severity, evidence, and recommended task?
- Does the provider also offer native work order tools if you do not run a CMMS?


Ask for a live demonstration, in your own test environment if possible, of one alert becoming one work order. The integration should support your[industrial maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/industrial-maintenance) workflow, not add a second one.


## Criterion 5: SLA and Accuracy Guarantees


Get the provider's SLA in writing and read how each term is measured. Platform uptime and support response times are the most common commitments; accuracy commitments are less common and only meaningful when "missed detection" and "false alarm" are defined.


Ask each provider:


- What platform uptime and support response times are committed, and what are the remedies if they are missed?
- How is a missed detection defined and reviewed?
- How are false alarms counted, and what happens when they pile up on one asset?
- Is the SLA the same for each site in a multi-site agreement?


Treat sales claims about accuracy as a starting point for questions. Your pilot results are the better evidence.


## Criterion 6: Support Model (24/7, Onboarding, Training)


Choose a provider whose support covers installation, training, and day-to-day questions from technicians, with clear hours and response times. Support matters most in the first months, when the team is still deciding whether to trust the alerts.


**Ask each provider:**


- Who installs the sensors, and is installation included in the price?
- What training do technicians, planners, and reliability engineers receive?
- Is there a named contact for your site after go-live?
- What are support hours, and is round-the-clock coverage available for critical alerts?
- Can you reach an analyst or engineer when an alert is unclear, and is that included or billed separately?


## Criterion 7: Pricing Transparency and Licensing Model


Choose a provider that can show the full multi-year cost on your asset list, including hardware, services, and renewals. Licensing is usually per sensor, per asset, or by site subscription, with hardware sometimes billed separately.


Ask each provider:


- What is the licensing unit, and how is an "asset" defined?
- Who pays for replacement sensors and batteries?
- Are installation, training, integration, and analyst support included?
- What are the minimum term, renewal, and price escalation terms?
- Who owns the data, and can you export it if you leave?


Our guide to[AI condition monitoring cost](https://tractian.com/en/blog/ai-condition-monitoring-cost) walks through budgeting and ROI math, and the[AI condition monitoring software buyer's guide](https://tractian.com/en/blog/ai-condition-monitoring-software) compares licensing models with a worked example.


## Provider Scorecard and Pilot Plan


Score finalists on the seven criteria, then confirm the scores with a pilot on your own assets. The scorecard keeps the comparison consistent; the pilot shows whether the provider's alerts hold up on your floor.


### Scorecard template


Rate each provider from 1 to 5 on each criterion and adjust the weights to your situation. The weights below are an illustrative starting point for a multi-site manufacturer, not a recommendation.


Criterion Example weight Provider A Provider B Provider C


1. Multimodal sensor coverage 20%


2. Edge deployment and connectivity 15%


3. Retrofit capability 15%


4. CMMS and ERP integration 15%


5. SLA terms 10%


6. Support model 15%


7. Pricing transparency 10%


**Weighted total** 100%


Before scoring, mark any hard requirements as pass/fail. A provider that cannot meet your network rules or hazardous area classification should drop out before the weighted total is calculated.


### Five steps for a provider pilot


1. **Pick the assets.** Choose a mix of critical machines and machines with known problems or recent failures, such as a pump with a history of seal leaks or a fan that trips on vibration.
2. **Agree on success criteria up front.** Write down what counts as a confirmed finding, a false alarm, and a missed fault, and how each will be verified.
3. **Install and integrate.** Have each provider install on comparable assets and connect alerts to your CMMS during the pilot, not after it.
4. **Verify alerts in the field.** Have technicians inspect flagged assets and record what they found. Feed that back to the provider and watch how they respond.
5. **Review with the full team.** Compare confirmed findings, false alarms, support responsiveness, and the quoted multi-year cost. Include the technicians who acted on the alerts.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Who offers scalable AI condition monitoring solutions for large fleets?


Providers that sell sensor-based AI condition monitoring with multi-site dashboards, including Tractian, are the usual candidates for large fleets. For fleet scale, check three things: whether pricing grows predictably per asset, whether each new site needs network work, and whether one view covers health across plants. Tractian's gateways relay data over 4G/LTE, which avoids a new plant network project at each site.


### Who offers turnkey AI condition monitoring packages including installation and training?


Several providers bundle sensors, connectivity, software, installation, and training, and Tractian is one of them. Its package includes Smart Trac Ultra sensors, gateways that relay data over 4G/LTE, the AI platform, installation and training by CMRP- and CAT-certified specialists, and native work order tools. Ask each provider for a written list of what is included and what is billed separately.


### Who supplies retrofit AI condition monitoring kits for legacy equipment?


Many sensor-based providers supply retrofit kits, including Tractian, whose wireless sensors mount externally on existing motors, pumps, fans, and gearboxes. When comparing kits, confirm mounting options, environment and hazardous area ratings, and how the provider handles machines with missing bearing or nameplate data. A good provider proposes sensing points per machine from your asset list.


### Which AI condition monitoring providers offer SLA-backed accuracy guarantees?


Written accuracy commitments are uncommon in this category, and their value depends on how missed detections and false alarms are defined. Request each provider's SLA document and compare the definitions, measurement method, and remedies. Platform uptime and support response times are the commitments you are most likely to find in writing.


### How to select an AI condition monitoring provider with 24/7 support and SLA guarantees?


Start by asking each provider for its SLA document and support policy, then compare support hours, response times by severity, escalation paths, and remedies. Confirm whether round-the-clock coverage applies to critical alerts or only to platform outages, and whether analyst or engineering support is included. Test responsiveness during the pilot by logging real questions and timing the answers.


### What AI condition monitoring tools integrate seamlessly with CMMS and ERP?


Look for tools with prebuilt connectors to your specific CMMS or ERP, an open API, and work orders that carry the asset ID, fault, severity, and evidence. Tractian connects through APIs to CMMS, ERP, SCADA, and APM systems, lists SAP, IBM Maximo, and Oracle NetSuite among its integrations, and also offers native work order tools. Ask any provider for a live demo of an alert becoming a work order in your system.


### What are the best entry-level AI condition monitoring platforms for small-to-medium businesses?


For a small or mid-sized plant, the best entry-level platform is one you can start on a handful of critical assets without new IT infrastructure or a resident vibration analyst. Look for wireless sensors with cellular connectivity, alerts that explain the fault in plain terms, included installation and training, and pricing that scales per asset. Start with a small group of critical machines and expand once technicians trust the alerts, a common path toward broader[predictive maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/predictive-maintenance) .


### How long does it take to deploy an AI condition monitoring provider's system?


Sensor installation usually takes minutes per asset, so most of the timeline goes to scoping, the model's learning period, and integration. Tractian's standard deployment gets customers fully operational within 14 days. CMMS or ERP integration and IT security review can extend that depending on your organization.


### What should I ask an AI condition monitoring provider in the first call?


Ask which signals their sensors measure, how data leaves the plant floor, how alerts reach your CMMS, what the SLA covers, who supports your technicians, and how pricing is calculated on your asset list. Those six answers tell you quickly whether a provider fits your plant.
